en.explanation:
Given,

$$\begin{aligned} & T=27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=300 \mathrm{~K} \\ & R=2 \mathrm{cal} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \end{aligned}$$

Reaction for combustion of carbon monoxide is given as:

$$\begin{gathered} \mathrm{CO}(g)+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2(g) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(g) \\ \therefore\quad \Delta n_g=1-1.5=-\frac{1}{2} \end{gathered}$$

Now, the difference between heat of combustion of carbon monoxide gas at constant pressure and at constant volume is given by

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta H-\Delta U & =\Delta n_g R T \\ \therefore \quad \Delta H-\Delta U & =-\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 300=-300 \mathrm{cal} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A stone is dropped into a pond. Waves in the form of circles are generated and radius of outermost ripple increases at the rate of $5 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{sec}$. Then area increased after 2 seconds is ............
en.explanation:
To determine the rate at which the area of the circular ripple increases, start by considering the formula for the area of a circle:

$$ A = \pi r^2 $$

where $ A $ is the area and $ r $ is the radius of the circle.

Given that the radius of the ripple increases at the rate of $ \frac{dr}{dt} = 5 \, \text{cm/sec} $, we want to find the rate of change of the area, $ \frac{dA}{dt} $, after 2 seconds.

First, apply the chain rule to differentiate the area with respect to time $ t $:

$$ \frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt} (\pi r^2) = 2\pi r \frac{dr}{dt} $$

After differentiating, substitute the known rate of change of the radius:

$$ \frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r \cdot 5 $$

Now, determine the radius after 2 seconds. Since the radius increases at a rate of $ 5 \, \text{cm/sec} $, after 2 seconds, the radius will be:

$$ r = 5 \times 2 = 10 \, \text{cm} $$

Substitute $ r = 10 \, \text{cm} $ into the expression for $ \frac{dA}{dt} $:

$$ \frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi \cdot 10 \cdot 5 = 100\pi \, \text{cm}^2/\text{sec} $$

Thus, the area increases at a rate of:

Option A: $ 100 \pi \, \text{cm}^2/\text{sec} $

en.content: A stone of mass 1 kg is tied to a string 2 m long and it's rotated at constant speed of $40 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ in a vertical circle. The ratio of the tension at the top and the bottom is [Take $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$]

Free body diagram (FBD) of a stone moving in a vertical circular path, which has tension force at point $A$ and $B$ as represented by $T_A$ and $T_B$ respectively as given below in the figure,

As, we know that the tension at position $A$,

$$\begin{aligned} & T_A=\frac{m v^2}{R}+m g \quad\left(\therefore F_c=\frac{m v^2}{R}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad T_A=\frac{1 \times(40)^2}{2}+1 \times 10=810 \mathrm{~N} \end{aligned}$$

$$\frac{T_B}{T_A}=\frac{790}{810}=\frac{79}{81}$$

Hence, the ratio of tension at position $B$ and tension at position $A$ is $79: 81$.

en.content: Two open pipes of different lengths and same diameter in which the air column vibrates with fundamental frequencies ' $n_1$ ', and ' $n_2$ ' respectively. When both pipes are joined to form a single pipe, its fundamental frequency will be

When both the pipes are joined together then net length of the pipe will be,

en.content: If ' $C_P$ ' and ' $C_V$ ' are molar specific heats of an ideal gas at constant pressure and volume respectively. If ' $\lambda$ ' is the ratio of two specific heats and ' $R$ ' is universal gas constant then ' $C_p$ ' is equal to

en.content: The quantity which does not vary periodically for a particle performing SHM is
en.explanation:

$$\begin{aligned} & =E_K+E_P=\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} k x^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{m}\left(A^2-x^2\right)+\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \\ & (\because v=\sqrt{A^2-x^2} \text { where, } A \text { is the } \\ & \text { amplitude of the particle) } \\ & =\frac{1}{2} K A^2 \end{aligned}$$

It is independent of $t, x$ is remains constant i.e., it does not vary periodically.

$$v=\frac{d x}{d t}=\omega \sqrt{A^2-x^2}$$

which varies with $x$.

Acceleration of the particle,

Which also varies with $x$.

en.content: Bohr model is applied to a particle of mass ' $m$ ' and charge ' $q$ ' is moving in a plane under the influence of a transverse magnetic field ' $B$ '. The energy of the charged particle in the $n$th level will be ( $h=$ Planck's constant)

$$\begin{aligned} \text { initial volume } & =\text { final volume } \\ V_{\text {initial }} & =\mathrm{V}_{\text {final }} \\ 2 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 & =1 \cdot \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \Rightarrow r=2^{1 / 3} R\quad \text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

As, surface tension is constant for both the drops.

So, the surface energy of two small drops,

$$E_1=2 \times T A_1=2 \times 4 \pi R^2 \times T$$

Surface energy of one big drop,

$$E_2=T A_2=4 \pi r^2 \times T=2^{1 / 3} .4 \pi R^2 T \text { (using Eq. (i)) }$$

Ratio the total surface energy before and after the change is given as,

$$\frac{E_1}{E_2}=\frac{8 \pi}{2^{2 / 3}} \frac{R^2 T}{4 \pi R^2 T}=\frac{2^{1-\frac{2}{3}}}{1}=2^{\frac{1}{3}}: 1$$

Hence, the ratio of surface energy of the each drop is $2^{\frac{1}{3}}: 1$.

en.content: If radius of the solid sphere is doubled by keeping its mass constant, the ratio of their moment of inertia about any of its diameter is
en.explanation:
Key Idea Moment of inertia of a solid sphere about its diameter is given as, $I=\frac{2}{5} M R^2$, where $M$ and $R$ are the mass and radius of the sphere, respectively.

Moment of inertia of a solid sphere about its diameter is $I=\frac{2}{5} M R^2\quad \text{.... (i)}$

As the radius of a solid sphere is doubled then the new moment of inertia of the sphere will be

$$I^{\prime}=\frac{2}{5} M(2 R)^2=\frac{8}{5} M R^2\quad\text{.... (ii)}$$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$\frac{I}{I^{\prime}}=\frac{\frac{2}{5} M R^2}{\frac{8}{5} M R^2}=\frac{1}{4}=1: 4$$

The ratio of their moment of inertia about any of its diameter is $1: 4$.

en.content: For a metallic wire, the ratio of voltage to corresponding current is

options.content: increases or decreases with rise in temperature depending upon the metal.

en.explanation:
According to Ohm's law, the ratio of the voltage to the corresponding current is represented as resistance i.e.,

$$\frac{V}{I}=R(\text { resistance })$$

For a metallic wire, with the increase in temperature the resistance also increase due to increased motion of the thermal electrons inside it.

en.content: In air, a charged soap bubble of radius ' $R$ ' breaks into 27 small soap bubbles of equal radius ' $r$ '. Then the ratio of mechanical force acting per unit area of big soap bubble to that of a small soap bubble is
en.explanation:
Key Idea The force per unit area is pressure Pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $R$. is given by

$$P=\frac{4 T}{R}$$

where, $T=$ surface tension and $\quad R=$ radius of the drop

Pressure inside a soap bubble, $P=\frac{4 T}{R}$.

If a bubble is break into 27 small soap bubbles then the volume of single bubble of radius $R$ and the combined volume of 27 bubbles of radius $r$ would be constant.

$27 \times$ volume of small bubbles $=$ volume of larger bubble

$$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & & 27\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3\right) & =\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \\ \Rightarrow & & 27 r^3 & =R^3 \\ \Rightarrow & & r & =\frac{R}{3}\quad \text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

Now, the pressure inside smaller soap bubble,

$$P_{\text {small }}=\frac{4 T}{r}=\frac{12 T}{R} \text { (using the relation) }$$

and similarly $P_{\text {large }}=\frac{4 t}{R}$

$\therefore$ Ratio of pressure of the smaller and larger soap bubble is given as,

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{P_{\text {larger }}}{P_{\text {small }}}=\frac{4 T}{R} \times \frac{R}{12 T}=\frac{1}{3} \\ P_{\text {larger }}: P_{\text {small }} & =1: 3 \end{aligned}$$

Hence, the ratio of mechanical force acting per unit area of big soap bubble to that of a small bubble is $1: 3$.

en.content: A layer of atmosphere that reflects medium frequency radio waves which is ineffective during night, is
en.explanation:
The atmospheric $E$ region or $E$ layer is above the $D$-region and below the F-region. It exists at altitude between 100 to 125 km above the earth surface $E$-layer assists in long distance radio communication.

en.content: A transverse wave is propagating on the string. The linear density of a vibrating string is $10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}$. The equation of the wave is $Y=0.05 \sin (x+15 t)$ where $x$ and $Y$ are measured in metre and time in second. The tension force in the string is
en.explanation:
Given that, the linear mass density,

$m=10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}$ and equation of the wave

$$y=0.05 \sin (x+15 t)\quad \text{.... (i)}$$

Since, the general equation of wave,

$$y=a \sin (k x+\omega t)\quad \text{... (ii)}$$

Now, compairing the Eqs. (i) and (ii) we get,

$$k=1, \lambda=2 \pi \quad\left(\because k=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}\right)$$

and $\omega=15 \Rightarrow f=\frac{15}{2 \pi} (\because \omega=2 \pi f)$

Velocity of the wave, $v=f \lambda=2 \pi \times \frac{15}{2 \pi}=15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

As, we know, the tension force in the string,

$$T=v^2 m \quad\left(\because v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}\right)$$

So, by substituting the values in the above relation, we get

$$T=(15)^2 \times 10^{-3}=0.225 \mathrm{~N}$$

Hence, the tension force in the string is 0.225 N.

en.content: The kinetic energy of a revolving satellite (mass $m$ ) at a height equal to thrice the radius of the earth $(R)$ is
en.explanation:
As we know that the kinetic energy of a revolving satellite at a height $h$ above the earth's surface is given as

$$\begin{aligned} K E=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 & =\frac{G M m}{2 r}\left(\because v=\frac{\sqrt{G M}}{r} \text { for circular orbit }\right) \\ & =\frac{G M m}{2(R+h)} \end{aligned}$$

where, R is the radius of the earth.

Given, height of a satellite from the earth surface $h=3 R$ and mass of the satellite $=m$

So,

$$\begin{aligned} & K E=\frac{G M m}{2(R+3 R)}=\frac{G M m}{2(4 R)} \\ & K E=\frac{G M m}{8 R} \times \frac{R}{R} \\ \therefore\quad & G M m \frac{R}{8 R^2}=\frac{g m R}{8} \quad\left(\therefore g=\frac{G M}{R^2}\right) \end{aligned}$$

So, the kinetic energy, $K E=\frac{g m R}{8}$.

en.content: A particle executes the simple harmonic motion with an amplitude ' $A$ '. The distance travelled by it in one periodic time is
en.explanation:
Key Idea One time period means the total time in which the particle returns to the same point and in the same direction from where it was released.

Now, in simple harmonic motion (SHM) total distance travelled is 4A.

This is because the particle covers $A$ in $\frac{T}{4}$ time period i.e., when it moves from $A$ to $B$, So in complete $T$ time it covers 4 times the amplitude distance i.e., $4 A$.

en.content: A galvanometer has resistance of $100 \Omega$ and a current of 10 mA produces full scale deflection in it. The resistance to be connected in series, to get a voltmeter of range 50 volt is
en.explanation:
A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter by connecting a resistance in series with the galvanometer as shown in the circuit diagram,

Given, galvanometer resistance, $R_G=100 \Omega$

Voltmeter range, $V_{\max }=50 \mathrm{~V}$ and full deflection current $I_f=10 \mathrm{~mA}$

So, by applying the $K V L$ in above circuit diagram,

$\therefore$ For a 50 V voltmeter range there must be,

Hence, the resistance to be connected in series, to get a voltmeter of range 50 V is $4900 \Omega$.

en.content: The angle made by orbital angular momentum of electron with the direction of the orbital magnetic moment is
en.explanation:
The relation between electron's angular momentum $L$ and magnetic moment $\mu$ given, $\mu=-\frac{e}{2 m_e} L$, where $e$ and $m_e$ are the charges and mass of the electron.

Here, negative sign shows that the angular momentum and magentic moment are in opposite direction to each other i.e., if $L$ in $+z$-direction then $\mu$ in-z-direction

en.content: The circuit in 1$$\Omega$$ resistor in the following circuit is
en.explanation:
Condition for balanced wheatstone-bridge,

$$\begin{array}{ll} & \frac{P}{Q}=\frac{R}{S} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{5}{1}=\frac{50}{10} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{5}{1}=\frac{5}{1} \end{array}$$

en.content: The wavelength of the first line in Balmer series in the hydrogen spectrum is ' $\lambda$ '. What is the wavelength of the second line in the same series?
en.explanation:
Wavelength in Balmer series of hydrogen spectrum is given by relation,

$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left[\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right] \quad \text { where, } n=3,4,5$$

So, wavelength of first line,

$$\begin{array}{rlr} \frac{1}{\lambda_1} & =R\left[\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{3^2}\right] \\ & =\frac{5 R}{36} \\ \Rightarrow \quad R & =\frac{36}{5 \lambda} & \left(\therefore \lambda_1=\lambda, \text { given) ..... (i)}\right) \end{array}$$

Similarly wavelength of second line,

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\lambda_2}=R\left[\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4^2}\right]=\frac{3 R}{16} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \lambda_2=\frac{16}{3 R}\quad \text{.... (ii)} \end{aligned}$$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$\lambda_2=\frac{20}{27} \lambda \text {. }$$

Hence, the wavelength of the second line in the same series is $\frac{20}{27} \lambda$.

en.content: Work done in stretching a wire through 1 mm is 2 J . What amount of work will be done for elongating another wire of same material, with half the length and double the radius of cross section, by 1 mm ?
en.explanation:
Given that, work done, $W=2 \mathrm{~J}$

As, we have two wires of same material and they are elongated to the same length.

So, this means, their Young's modulus $(Y)$ is same and $\Delta I_1=\Delta I_2=\Delta I$ (say)

The work done in stretching a wire,

$$W=\frac{1}{2} F \Delta I$$

Now, for both the wires we have

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{W_1}{W_2}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} F_1 \Delta l}{\frac{1}{2} F_2 \Delta l} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & W_2=2 \times \frac{F_2}{F_1}\quad \text{.... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

The forces by which the wires are stretched can be expressed as the ratio,

$$\begin{gathered} \frac{F_1}{F_2}=\frac{Y A_1 \frac{\Delta I}{L_1}}{Y A_2 \frac{\Delta I}{L_2}} \\ =\frac{r_1^2 L_2}{r_2^2 L^2}\quad\text{... (ii)} \end{gathered}$$

Given, $r_2=2 r_1$ and $L_2=\frac{L_4}{2}$

Now, substituting the given values in Eq. (ii), we get

$$\frac{F_1}{F_2}=\frac{r_1^2 L_1}{4 r_1^2 2 L_2}=\frac{1}{8}\quad\text{.... (iii)}$$

From Eqs. (i) and (iii), we get

$$\begin{aligned} W_2 & =2 \times 8 \\ & =16 \mathrm{~J} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: A uniform rod of length ' 6 L ' and mass ' 8 m ' is pivoted at its centre ' $C$ '. Two masses ' $m$ ' and ' $2 m^{\prime}$ with speed $2 v, v$ as shown strikes the rod and stick to the rod. Initially the rod is at rest. Due to impact, if it rotates with angular velocity ' $\omega$ ' then ' $\omega$ ' will be
en.explanation:
A rod of length 6L and mass 8 m is given in figure,

When two masses strike the rod, then angular momentum imparted to rod,

$$\begin{aligned} L_1+L_2 & =2 m v(L)+m(2 v)(2 L) \\ & =6 m v L \end{aligned}$$

Now, after striking of masses to rod the angular momentum of complete rod about the centre $C$,

$$L_{\text {od }}=10\quad \text{... (i)}$$

where, $\omega=$ angular velocity of the rod

and $\quad I=$ moment of inertia of the rod.

The moment of inertia of rod

$$I=\frac{M I^2}{12}=\frac{8 m(6 L)^2}{12}=24 m L^2$$

$\therefore M=8 \mathrm{~m}$ and $I=6 L$ (given)

Now, moment of inertia of two masses after the striking to $I$ rod

$$I_1=2 m(L)^2=2 m L^2$$

and $$I_2=m(2 L)^2=4 m L^2$$

$\therefore$ The net moment of the inertia about the centre of rod,

$$\begin{aligned} & I=24 m L^2+2 m L^2+4 m L^2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & I=30 \mathrm{~mL}^2 \end{aligned}$$

By putting this value in Eq. (i), we get

$$L_{\text {rod }}=30 M L^2 \omega$$

From the law of conservation of angular momentum,

$$\begin{aligned} & & L_1+L_2 & =L_{\text {rod }} \\ \Rightarrow & & 6 m v L & =30 m L^2 \omega \\ \Rightarrow & & \omega & =\frac{v}{5 L} \end{aligned}$$

Hence, the anguler velocity of the rod is $\frac{v}{5 L}$.

en.content: A thin metal wire of length 'L' and uniform linear mass density '$\rho$' is bent into a circular coil with 'O' as centre. the moment of inertia of a coil about the axis XX' is
en.explanation:

Moment of inertia of a thin circular coil,

en.content: The dimensions of torque are same as that of
en.explanation:
Torque is expressed as,

$\tau=$ force $(F) \times$ perpendicular distance $(r)$

So,

$$\begin{aligned} {[\tau] } & =[F] \times[r]=\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right][\mathrm{L}] \\ & =\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right] \end{aligned}$$

As, the torque has dimension $\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$, which is correctly matched by the dimensions of moment of force. So, option (a) is correct.

en.content: A clock pendulum having coefficient of linear expansion. $\alpha=9 \times 10^{-7} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$ has a period of 0.5 s at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the clock is used in a climate, where the temperature is $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, how much time does the clock lose in each oscillation? ( $g=$ constant)
en.explanation:
Given, the coefficient of linear expansion,

$$\alpha=9 \times 10^{-7 \circ} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$$

Initial time period, $T_0=0.5 \mathrm{~s}$, initial temperature $T_i=20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and final temperature, $T_f=30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

Expansion in length, $\Delta l=l \alpha\left(T_f-T_i\right)$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \Delta l=l \times 9 \times 10^{-7}(30-20)$$

Now, the time period of pendulum,

$$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$$

Error in time period,

$$\frac{\Delta t}{T}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta l}{l}+\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta g}{g}$$

Since, $\Delta g=0$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta T}{T}=\frac{1 \Delta l}{2} \frac{\Delta l}{l}$$

Now, substituting values in the above equation, we get,

$$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta T}{0.5}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1 \times 9 \times 10^{-7}}{1}(30-20)\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \Delta T=\frac{0.5 \times 9 \times 10^{-7} \times 10}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \Delta T=2.25 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~s} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Two capillary tubes of different diameters are dipped in water. The rise of water is

options.content: more in the tube of larger diameter.
more in the tube of smaller diameter.

en.explanation:
The rise of water in a capillary tube is expressed as, $h=\frac{2 T \cos \theta}{r d g}$

where, $h=$ height of the capillary rise, $T=$ surface tension, $r=$ radius of the capillary tube, $g=$ gravitational acceleration and $d=$ density of the liquid Here, $T, d$ and, $g$ remain constant.

So, $h \propto \frac{1}{r}$

The rise of water is more in the tube of smaller radius.

en.content: A body is projected vertically from the surface of the earth of radius ' $R$ ' with velocity equal to half of the escape velocity. The maximum height reached by the body is
en.explanation:
According to the law of conservation of energy,

$$\begin{aligned} & (\text { Total energy) })_{\text {surtace }}=(\text { Total energy })_{\text {(max height) }} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad(K E+P E)_{\text {surtace }}=(K E+P E)_{\max \text { height }} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m v^2+\left(-\frac{G M m}{R}\right)=0+\left(-\frac{G M m}{R+h}\right) \end{aligned}$$

Given, $\quad v=\frac{1}{2} v_e=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} m\left[\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{2 G M}{R}\right]-\frac{G M m}{R}=-\frac{G M m}{R+h}$

$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{4} \frac{G M m}{R}-\frac{G M m}{R}=-\frac{G M m}{R+h}$

$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1-4}{4 R}=\frac{1}{R+h} \Rightarrow 3 R+3 h=4 R$

$\Rightarrow \quad h=\frac{R}{3}$

So, option (b) is the correct answer.

en.content: In biprism experiment, the distance between source and eyepiece is 1.2 m, the distance between two virtual sources is 0.84 mm. Then the wavelength of light used if eyepiece is to be moved transversely through a distance of 2.799 cm to shift 30 fringes is

where, $\beta$ is the fringe width,

$d$ is the distance between the two sources and $D$ is the distance between the source and eyepeice.

Substituting these values in Eq. (i), we get

$$\begin{aligned} \lambda & =\frac{0.84 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.33 \times 10^{-4}}{1.2} \\ & =6.531 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}=6531 \mathop A\limits^o \end{aligned}$$

en.content: When photons of energy $h v$ fall on a metal plate of work function ' $W_0$ ', photoelectrons of maximum kinetic energy ' $K$ ' are ejected. If the frequency of the radiation is doubled, the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectrons will be
en.explanation:
Given, energy of photon $=h \nu$, work function $=W_0$ and maximum kinetic energy $=K$

So, from the Einstein's photoelectric equation,

$$\begin{aligned} & E=K+W_0 \Rightarrow h v=K+W_0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad K=h v-W_0\quad \text{... (i)} \end{aligned}$$

If frequency of the radiation is doubled, then Einstein's photoelectric equation changed as

$$K^{\prime}=h(2 v)-W_0\quad \text{... (ii)}$$

By substracting the Eq. (i) from (ii), we get

$$\begin{aligned} K^{\prime}-K & =h(2 v)-h v-W_0+W_0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K^{\prime} & =K+h v \end{aligned}$$

So, option (b) is correct.

en.content: The magnitude of the magnetic induction at a point on the axis at a large distance ( $r$ ) from the centre of a circular coil of ' $n$ ' turns and area ' $A$ ' carrying current ( $I$ ) is given by
en.explanation:
As we know that the magnetic field on the axis of a circular current carrying loop,

$$B=\frac{\mu_0 n / a^2}{2\left(r^2+a^2\right)^{3 / 2}}\quad \text{.... (i)}$$

where, $I=$ current through the coil, $a=$ radius of a circular loop, $r=$ distance of point from the centre along the axis and $n=$ number of turns in the coil.

Area of the coil, $A=\pi a^2$

$$\Rightarrow \quad a^2=\frac{A}{\pi}\quad\text{.... (ii)}$$

and it $r \gg a$ then, $\left(r^2+a^2\right)^{3 / 2} \approx r^3\quad \text{... (iii)}$

From Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & B=\left(\frac{\mu_0 n I}{2 r^3}\right) \frac{A}{\pi} \times \frac{2}{2} \\ & B=\frac{2 \mu_0 n / A}{4 \pi r^3} \end{array}$$

So, option (b) is correct.

en.content: A metal sphere of radius ' $R$ ' and density ' $\rho_1$ ' is dropped in a liquid of density ' $\sigma$ ' moves with terminal velocity ' $v$ '. Another metal sphere of same radius and density ' $\rho_2$ ' is dropped in the same liquid, its terminal velocity will be
en.explanation:
The terminal velocity of the sphere

$$v=\frac{2}{9} R^2 \frac{\left(\rho_1-\sigma\right) g}{\eta}\quad \text{.... (i)}$$

Here, $R=$ radius of sphere, $\rho_1=$ density of sphere and $\sigma=$ density of liquid.

Now, if density of metal sphere is changed to $\rho_2$, then terminal velocity

$$v_2=\frac{2}{9} \frac{R^2\left(\rho_2-\sigma\right) g}{\eta}\quad\text{... (ii)}$$

Divide Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$\frac{v_2}{v}=\frac{\left(\rho_2-\sigma\right)}{\left(\rho_1-\sigma\right)} \text { or } v_2=\frac{v\left(\rho_2-\sigma\right)}{\left(\rho_1-\sigma\right)}$$

Hence, the terminal velocity is $\frac{v\left(\rho_2-\sigma\right)}{\rho_1-\sigma}$.

en.content: If $\alpha$ is the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator and ' $Q$ ' is heat released to the hot reservoir, then the heat extracted from the cold reservoir ' $Q_2$ ' is
en.explanation:
As we know that the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator,

$$\begin{aligned} & \alpha=\frac{Q_2}{W} \quad \left(\therefore W=Q_1-Q_2\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \alpha=\frac{Q_2}{Q_1-Q_2}\quad \text{... (i)}\end{aligned}$$

where, $Q_2=$ heat extracted from the cold reservoir, $Q_1=$ heat released to the hot reservoir, $W=$ work done by heat pump and $\alpha=$ coefficient of performance

So, $\alpha\left(Q_1-Q_2\right)=Q_2$ (from Eq. (i))

$$\Rightarrow \quad Q_2=\frac{\alpha Q_1}{1+\alpha}$$

en.content: The real force ' $F$ ' acting on a particle of mass $m$ ' performing circular motion acts along the radius of circle ' $r$ ' and is directed towards the centre of circle. The square root of magnitude of such force is ( $T=$ periodic time)
en.explanation:
Force $F$ acting on a body of mass $m$ peforming circular motion of radius $r$,

$$F=\frac{m v^2}{r} \quad \text { (centripetal force) }\quad\text{.... (i)}$$

where, $\quad v=$ velocity of the particle The time period of one complete cycle,

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & T=\frac{\text { perimeter of a circular path }}{\text { velocity of body }}=\frac{2 \pi r}{v} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & v=\frac{2 \pi r}{T}\quad \text{... (ii)} \end{array}$$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$F=\frac{m}{r}\left(\frac{2 \pi r}{T}\right)^2=m r\left(\frac{2 \pi}{T}\right)^2 \text { or } \sqrt{F}=\frac{2 \pi}{T} \sqrt{m r}$$

So, option (a) is correct.

en.content: Dimensions of Gyromagnetic ratio are
en.explanation:
Gyromagnetic ratio is the ratio of magnetic dipole moment of revolving electron to its angular momentum,

i.e $\frac{\mu}{L}=\frac{e}{2 m_e}=$ gyromagnetic ratio

$$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & {\left[\frac{\mu}{L}\right]=\frac{[\text { current } \times \text { time }]}{[\text { mass }]}=\frac{[\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{T}]}{[\mathrm{m}]}} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\left[\frac{\mu}{L}\right]=\left[M^{-1} L^0 T^1 A^1\right] \quad(\because \text { Current, } I=A) \end{aligned}\\ &\text { Hence, the dimension of }\left(\frac{\mu}{L}\right) \text { is }\left[M^{-1} L^{\circ} T I\right] \end{aligned}$$

en.content: The maximum velocity of the photoelectron emitted by the metal surface is ' $v$ '. Charge and mass of the photoelectron is denoted by ' $e$ ' and ' $m$ ' respectively. The stopping potential in volt is
en.explanation:
Given, maximum velocity of a photoelectron $=v$

charge of photoelectron $=e$

and mass of photoelectron $=m$.

Let, the stopping potential of the photoelectron $=V$,

Then, the maximum kinetic energy

en.content: The equi-convex lens has a focal length ' $f$ '. If the lens is cut along the line perpendicular to the principal axis and passing through the pole, what will be the focal length of any half part?
en.explanation:
The lens Maker's formula is given as

$$\frac{1}{f}=\left(\mu_{\text {med }}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$

where, $f=$ focal length of lens, $R_1=$ radius of first curved part and $R_2=$ Radius of second curved part

As, for equiconvex lens $R_1=R_2=R$ (say)

So, $\quad \frac{1}{f}=\left(\mu_{\text {real }}-1\right) \frac{2}{R}\quad\text{... (i)}$

Now, if lens is cut along the line perpendicular to the principal axis as shown in the figure,

The new cut part of the lens has, $R_1=R$ and $R_2=\infty$ Again by using the lens Maker's formula, focal length of the new part of the lens,

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{f^{\prime}}=\left(\mu_{\text {real }}-1\right)\left[\frac{1}{R}-\left(-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{f}=\left(\mu_{\text {real }}-1\right)\left[\frac{1}{R}\right]\quad\text{... (ii)}\end{aligned}$$

So, from the Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$$f^{\prime}=2 f$$
